Write a dramatic short story with a shocking plot twist based on this prompt:

Suddenly Odin, Thor and other deities of the Norse mythologies reveal themselves to the world. They urge the world powers to mobilize their armies... for Ragnarök.

I guess I realized something was up when winter wouldn't stop. I mean, a straight year of snow and ice and below-freezing weather? Scientists were befuddled, that's for sure. Whatever happened to global warming? 
 
 Everybody had their own theories about what was happening - God's divine punishment, a disruption in the space-time continuum, whatever you could possibly think of. With my degree in Mythology, I thought of something else entirely. I thought of Fimbulvetr. Of the fabled story of a neverending winter. 
 
 It took some convincing, but after many debates and nights spent on the couch, my wife let me name our daughter Lif. Just a precaution, in case my premonition was true. 
 
 When Lif was three years old, the rooster's call was heard all over the world. There was no denying it now. I had been right - the world was ending. *Ragnarok* was here. 
 
 I can only hope that my daughter will survive.

The evil villain is not like other typical villains. Their plans are actually evil, and there traps aren't easily bypassed. They don't even explain their plan to the Hero. Who, in turn, can't believe he is being bested by an 8 year old.

" Jacob?" 
 
 The man stood with a furtive glance around the room, but he was alone except for the woman standing at the door. "Come on in," she said, holding the door for Jacob. "I was expecting someone, ah, younger. I'm Dr Felix." "Yes, um, well, I have a bit of a prediciment that I need help with and had the means to hire your services. Your secretary said it was unusual but that you wouldn't likely refuse." "Oh?" "I'm sure you've heard, you must have by now." Jacob sat awkwardly in the small chair in Dr Felix's office. "The terror attacks around the city. The government is shaking in their boots, but there's been no demands yet." "Ah, yes. The bombings around the schools and museums." "Yes, that." "And why has that brought you here?" "Well, I've been tracking the perpetrator, independantly. I'm hoping I can catch them and bring them down. See, I have a background in MMA and a passion for weapons, self defense, all that. Plus, I inherited a fair bit from some relatives when they passed away, so I don't have to worry about work. The police, RCMP, Military, they all have their own things to worry about, hoops to jump through, processes to follow. Not me, I'm independant." Jacob stretched his arms, feeling the half-healed sores on his back pull tightly. "I see, Jacob. However I'm still confused as to what has brought you to see me, a child psychaiatrist." "Well, that's just it. I've met the guy, well girl, who's doing it all. She's eight." 
 
 Dr Felix sat up in her chair. "What? Surely you're mistaken." 
 
 Jacob shook his head. "I wish I were. I met her a few weeks ago. I managed to get to Forest Valley Elementary before they finished evacuating. At first I thought she was a student who hadn't evacuated, but, well, she set me straight on that right quick." "What happened?" "She showed me where the bombs were. Ten in all, strategically placed throughout the school to maximize damage and ensure that the school wouldn't be able to reopen. Then she locked me in the middle of it all. Not that she told me anything. She didn't say a word." "How did you escape? I thought Forest Valley was flattened." "It was. I picked the lock and managed to make it into the staff room fridge before the bombs went off. Ended up in the hospital for a few days after that for the damage the shrapnel did to my back, but otherwise unharmed." 
 
 Dr Felix couldn't muster any words. 
 
 Jacob twisted his hands on his knees. "I next met her at the Science and Technology Museum. I went there looking for her, knowing that's where she'd be next. I mapped it out, see, she's doing a spiral around Captal Hill. I found her, there, just wandering and looking at different exhibits. I recognized her immediately and she recognized me. She stopped and waited until I caught up with her. I asked her how old she was and she held up eight fingers. I asked if she could speak and she nodded, read, another nod, write, a nod. I asked her if she went to school and she shook her head. Asked her if she used to go to school and she shook her head. Asked her what she was doing at the museum and she just smiled and ran away. I tried to catch up, but she was gone. Then the announcements came on to evacuate the building. I saw her once more that day, in the crowd of evacuated people, just standing and watching, smile on her face. But not a single word, nothing." "Oh my." Dr Felix had put her hand over her mouth in shock. "So now you see why I'm here. I don't need an assesmet for myself. I need help. I need to understand the how and why of this little girl, what her motives might be, and how I can communicate with her better." Jacob sniffed. "I want to help her. She must be hurting." 
 
 Dr Felix nodded and pulled out her notepad. "Let's get started. Together, we might be able to make a difference, somehow." "What do you need to know? I've talked to her a few times, but still not got a word from her. I've followed her some and know where she goes and how she gets around." "Let's start with how she bahaves around you." "Well, she seems to like me, but she shrinks back from me a bit. Whenever I lift my hand, even so high as my pocket, she flinches." "Okay, anything else?" The doctor scribbled something on her paper. "When I get down on my knee, get to her level she... 
 
 -- -- - "Hi." Jacob stopped some distance back from where the eight year old terror was standing in the classroom at Kanata Acadamy. 
 
 She turned toward him. The book in her hand slid to the floor. "You seem to not like places of learning." She shook her head. "Did your caregiver tell you about them?" She smiled and ran from the room. 
 
 Jacob ran after her, but by the time he got out the door, she was gone. "Shit." He ran out of the school, explosions chasing him down the hallway.

Upon death your soul travels to Valhalla (or Folkvangr), only to find that you have no means to defend yourself, as your family assumed your soul was destined for Hel and burned no weapons on your pyre.

I took pride in my work. I was the man who would defend the onslaught of punches and strikes thrown my way. The man who could launch his own right back at them. A man with millions behind me, united for my cause. The people loved me, but there was some who hated me. These people favoured other men in place of mine. But I need not fear of losing. 
 
 I made sure I always knew who I was up against, to make sure that those who posed a threat, became those that HAD posed a threat. 
 
 One day a very meager and simple looking man began to oppose me, he was working his way up. People gather behind him and the momentum did not stop. I tried everything I could to sully his name, blackmail him, surprise him with random warrants. I could not do it. Finally I stood face to face with him. 
 
 Then the world was black. 
 
 As I came to, I gazed around. A starry celestial sky filled my eyes and a great building stood in the distance. I started to walk towards it. 
 
 I made my way down a forest path laden with rocks and infested with vines. Tree roots provided the stumbling block I did not need to fall flat on my face. I brushed myself off and made my way forward towards a clearing, a break in the forest. 
 
 Two men stepped into clearing, one garbed in leather and wielding a sword, while the other held an assault rifle; adorned in what looked like military wear. "He doesn't have anything to defend himself with," spoke the man with the sword, "put down your arms." "Are we really gon na do this again? Last time we just ended up mildly inconvenienced and it wasn't really that fun," the soldier mumbled apathetically." "Yes. Come now little man, it is time for your undoing. "I had faced quick men, strong men, men who were excellent at evading my tactics, men who weren't so excellent at doing the same. I believe that I only lost to one man, the simple looking man. I will not let these dumb fools kill me. I don't know where I am, or who they are, but I will beat their ass down, or my name isn't Floyd Mayweather.

IF013 - Orbit

" I don't like it," said Grant, staring out the airlock as it opened, revealing the daunting planet below. 
 
 Harkins sighed from the other side of the room, holding a button down to complete the door's process. "There's no other way," he said. "Planetary defenses will shoot us down before we even make it into the atmosphere." He walked over to Grant by the doorway and patted his spacesuit on the shoulder. "What if she's not there?" asked Grant, not taking his eyes off the bluish planet below. "How will we even get back up here? Hell, even if we *find* her, how will we get her back up here?" 
 
 Harkins stood beside Grant and looked down with him. "She's down there, Grant. Don't ask me how I know. She's my sister and I *know* we're close." 
 
 Grant looked at Harkins and nearly wept at his confident stance. And then he looked back down. "Can we even make it without burning up?" "We'll make it," answered Harkins. "I designed these suits myself. They can counter the reentry speeds and keep us cool enough to make it. The chutes should do the rest." "You've never done this before, have you?" asked Grant, unsure he wanted to know the answer. "It's called a leap of faith for a reason," he responded. "She's your wife, Grant. This is the best lead we've gotten so far. You have to decide *now*." 
 
 Grant jumped out of the airlock without another moment's hesitation. Harkins let out a chuckle and jumped out after him.

Write a dramatic short story with a shocking plot twist based on this prompt:

Every time you die, you get to choose what you'll be reincarnated as. You've chosen ant 4 billion times.

Minim transmigrates, skitters, walks the intricate labyrinth of an entirely new colony. The tunnels branch out five-dimensionally, and far behind her is the distant memory of dying. She has emerged from her carapace a being of perfect and immortal soul, and the substrata of the world have revealed themselves to her. She crawls past matter, past space, past time, and in the fungal garden comes to rest. *Nigoda* swarm around her, single-celled souls so undifferentiated that they compose the base matter of the cosmos. She is afloat in a sea of life and death, of eternal rebirth. All possibilities are open to her. "And what shall you choose?" comes a waft of pheromones, and before her is the distended body of the queen, Tirthankara, all six legs folded in lotus formation, every segmented piece of her body a further elaboration of truth. Mimin feels her soul seize with the possibilities. Beyond one tunnel lies the unbound flight of the falcon, and she can peer down it to the glint of sun off the tops of clouds. There is the lotus emerging pure through the river mud. There is the antelope bounding gracefully through the plains. There is the crocodile with its slow and unnerving grin, snaking lazily through the waters. There is the elephant, there is the horse, there is the buffalo, there is the boar, there is the porcupine and the tortoise and monkey and the snake, a seemingly endless number of tiers of existence blurring indiscriminately into the looping circle of life. "Which of these are worthy of me?" trembles Minim, shaky on her fragile six legs. "Which do I deserve?" "There is neither retribution nor reward in death," Tirthankara says, her abdomen shining with light. "You, you yourself, are an intrinsically perfect soul, striving ever onward towards liberation. Only your actions, only your choices, shall determine what happens next." "I... I only sought to serve while I lived," says Minim, struggling to remember. "My sisters, they foraged and guarded us. While I tended to the gardens." She remembers tending to the delicate sprouts of fungus as they sprouted from the rotting leaves, heedful of their chemical songs of fruition, rearranging the leaf beds for maximum growth, hauling away the waste. "I could not have -" The thought confounds her, and she looks up to Tirthankara. "I was a limb in a greater organism." She looks to the mammalian paths of rebirth, twisting and turning all the way to the end until she can feel the concept of them worming through her mind. "A teat, a hand on a breast." She can almost feel the sensation of a heart beating, of warm blood flowing through her limbs. "If I were to be reborn... could I be something more?" "You could be as a demi-god," Tirthankara says, extending her limbs. "You could be as a being of hell." There are visions of creatures Minim has never imagined, never conceived of, standing vertically towards the sky. They stare through transparent eyes and incinerate dozens with a gaze. They extend many-toothed limbs and chew trees to the ground. They have built colonies of stone and smoke and fire that extend over the surface of the world. They could crush her and her colony with a single step. "You could stride atop the world. You could reach for the heavens. There are no limits imposed upon you here, sister. The choice is eternally yours." 
 
 Minim sees, and shudders with vertigo. She has lived a life without leaving her colony, without seeing the sun, and now she sees before her the possibility to harness the sun for herself, or to blot it from the sky. "I-" she gasps, and collapses back. "Forgive me," she whispers, and thinks of her precious gardens, moist and warm and dark and rich with fungus song, of the rows of squirming hungry children awaiting her care. There are her sisters who roved the edges of the colony, foraging for food, fighting off all enemies, whose bodies fed the gardens when they died. There was the queen, eternally birthing, the supple young drones readied to birth colonies anew. Her family. Her body. Her life. At the mercy of all the gods and demons she had just witnessed. "I wish to be me," she says. "I am no god. I am no demon. I - I wish to serve. Tiny though I may be in the larger scheme of things. I wish to help them be better." 
 
 Tirthankara beams, and the world slowly narrows down to a single familiar path. "You have trod this path well, sister," Tirthankara says. "Now walk it again." "Wait!" Minim gasps, and already she feels the constraints of a new physical form closing in around her. She is limbless, sightless. "How many times? How many times have I chosen this path?" "Four billion times," says Tirthankara. "And you shall walk it four billion times more. All paths are interconnected, sister. Your existence is entwined with air and earth and fire, with water and all the plants that grow. Seek to do no one harm, sister. Cultivate no attachments. Open yourself to the infinite possibilities of life." There is joy in Tirthankara's pheromonal voice. "Walk your path, sister, with ceaseless effort and free of delusions! And it shall lead you to liberation!" 
 
 And Minim transmigrates to a different plane on a thousand skittering feet, and she is born and dies and is born and dies and is born and dies and is reborn.

Glad to have ya in this here tourney. There's two things you need to know: First, if yer caught cheatin ', you'll be shot. Second, everyone cheats.

Avery Mason stared at his cards in dismay. His stack of chips had slowly been dwindling over the past hour as he folded hand after hand. He thought back to the words that the Judge had spoke to him when he first sat down. 
 
 *Everyone cheats. * 
 
 Avery stared at the rat faced man sitting across from him. His pencil thin mustache twitched as he pushed another four hundred dollars worth of chips into the pot. "I raise ya," he said softly. 
 
 Avery slipped the three aces out of his sleeve, making a show of rolling his sleeves up to display his bare arms and simultaneously hide the cards he swapped out. "I'm all in." 
 
 Avery pushed his small stack of chips into the center of the table. He stared down the rat faced man and waited, it was all about timing. As the words "call" left the other man's mouth Avery flipped his cards revealing his full house, aces and kings. The rat faced man was a second too slow. The dealer gasped when he saw both hands on the table. Everyone stared at the six aces on the table. "You cheatin' son of a bitch!" Avery shouted standing to draw his pistol. The mustached man tried to stand but a firm hand held him in place. He looked up to the bearded Judge. "What do we have here?" the Judge asked the table. "He's been pulling cards all game," Avery said in accusation. 
 
 The rest of the table nodded in agreement. The man had been having incredible "luck". The Judge picked him up and tore the man's jacket off. Cards cascaded out of his torn jacket to the floor. "No! It was him!" he pleaded as they dragged him across the wooden floor and out the back door. He screamed one more time before the gunshot silenced him. 
 
 One down, four to go. The dealer picked up the chips and placed them in front of himself. 
 
 The Judge's spurs clanged against the floor as he walked up to the table. "Play," he said gruffly. 
 
 The dealer shuffled and dealt the cards again. For the first time in the tournament Avery was getting decent cards. Money was moving quickly as each hand was played out. Everyone at the table was too nervous with trying to cheat as boldly as they had been before. Avery's stack of chips steadily grew as did his confidence. 
 
 One by one the men at the table ran out of money and got up from the table. Until it was just Avery and Willem left. Willem was a younger man with bright blonde hair and a charming smile. He had been playing a safe game. Avery had not seen the young man cheat yet. Either Willem wasn't cheating at all, or he was the best Avery had ever seen. Willem seemed to know exactly what Avery was holding every hand. It was a massacre. Avery's stack of chips was cut in half in one hand, from there it was downhill. Sweat was running down his back in a torrent. It had taken Avery months to steal enough money to sit at this table, he was damned if he was going to lose to this young upstart. Avery was trying to work the cards but every time Willem had a better hand. With a scowl he watched the dealer throw out what he knew would be his final hand, and that's when he saw it. The son of a bitch. 
 
 Avery shifted in his seat and eased the small pistol out of his left boot and pressed it into the dealer's knee underneath the table. The dealer met Avery's eyes and swallowed deeply. He got the message. Avery folded without even looking at the cards in front of him. The dealer reshuffled and dealt. 
 
 Avery tipped the corner of the cards and saw pocket aces. "All in," Avery said pushing his small stack into the center of the table. "Call," Willem said with a grin, "nice playing with you old timer." 
 
 Avery's aces beat Willem's kings. The tide had turned and Avery pulled the pistol from the dealers knee. Cards flew and chips went back and forth, but now it was more evenly matched. Willem figured out after a few hands that the dealer was no longer helping him cheat. It was an honest game. Something the young man hadn't played in a long time. 
 
 Avery grinned as he won another massive pot. "I don't know how you are cheating old man, but as soon as I see I'm going to shoot you right between your eyes," Willem threatened. 
 
 The Judge stood over the table watching with a keen eye. "Only thing I see happening is you losing young man," Avery replied. 
 
 The cards were dealt again. Before he looked at them Avery knew he was going to win this hand. He felt it in every fiber of his body. Lady luck blew a seductive kiss his way. 
 
 Willem pushed his last chips into the center of the table. He knew he couldn't muscle the big stack, this was a play of desperation. 
 
 Avery loosened the gun on his hip out of the holster as he called. 
 
 Willem stood before the cards finished falling to the table, the barrel of his six shooter climbing in slow motion. Avery pulled the trigger before Willem even got his pistol up. Willem's knee shattered as the bullet passed through it. The second round took him in between the eyes as he was collapsing to the floor. 
 
 Avery turned the pistol on the dealer and shot him for good measure. "Mighty fine game," the Judge said. "Thanks. You can take that stupid beard off now, you look ridiculous," Avery replied. "I thought it made me look distinguished," The Judge said with a hint of hurt feelings. "Good job on the card drop by the way, that rat faced jack ass never saw it coming," Avery said with a grin. "Thanks," the Judge said pulling the beard off and letting it fall to the floor. "C'mon brother, this town is shot. Time to find a few more suckers," Avery said placing the stacks of cash into his bag. 
 
 The two brothers walked out of the saloon and into the night.

“ Just talk it out Tom! Tell me how you feel! ” 
 
 “ I don ’ t wan na talk about it, ok? ” 
 
 This conversation is anything but unfamiliar. Tom works his butt off for his wife and kid. I mean really hard: overtime, weekends, during intergalactic holidays.
